# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-2 (Extended v57)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; 1809 (Pope's arrest); 1811 (Bishop's synod); 1813 onward (Napoleon's decline); 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, early October—evening/night of Valjean's theft and flight; **Battle of Waterloo/Hougomont siege, June 17-18, 1815**); 1817 (carrier sighting; young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil cook-shop, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral appointment and town transformation); **1823 January (Fantine's arrest and street incident; Javert's revelation; Valjean's acute crisis; TRIAL SEQUENCE: Journey to Arras through February, arriving evening near eight o'clock; TRIAL EVENING SESSION; witnesses testify; Valjean reveals himself; acquittal of Champmathieu; arrest order issued; RETURN TO M. SUR M. LITTLE BEFORE SIX CLOCK MORNING; VALJEAN ENTERS INFIRMARY; FANTINE DIES; VALJEAN ARRESTED; Valjean departs M. sur M. marching toward Paris carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse)**; 1849 (chapel walls freshly whitewashed); 1861/1862 (narrative reflection, traveller departing from Nivelles toward La Hulpe); **summer of the first year** (present narrative time); future wedding (following spring)
- Primary locations: M. sur M.; Montfermeil; Arras; Nivelles; La Hulpe; Braine-l'Alleud; Lillois; Genappe; Hal; Tongres; **Hougomont (château, farm, chapel, well, orchard, garden, wood, northern and southern doors, paddock, spiral staircase, chapel with wooden crucifix and Saint Anne statue); Mont-Saint-Jean plateau; Belle-Alliance; Abbey of Villiers forest; Rossomme farm; village of Ohain; hollow road of Ohain (from Braine-l'Alleud); Chapelle-Saint-Lambert; Wavre; Dion-le-Mont; Plancenoit; forest of Paris; Papelotte; Frischemont; Boitsfort; Groenendael; Soignes forest; Waterloo battlefield**; England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere, Dunby, Yarlby, Ostcombe, Ravenmere); Kelmere (river crossing); English harbor town of Dunstead; meadow near Genappe; willow at Wilwick; forge; Vincennes; Schoenbrunn; Philippi

## Waterloo Battle: Strategic Analysis, Conditions, Course, Outcome, and Philosophical Meaning

**Napoleon's Military Philosophy and Battle Plan**
- Artillery officer by training; victory method: converge artillery on single point, overwhelm weak points with grape-shot
- Plan (masterpiece by all confession): proceed straight to centre of Allies' line, make breach, cut them in two, drive British half back on Hal and Prussian half on Tongres, carry Mont-Saint-Jean, seize Brussels
- **Counterfactual**: had soil been dry and artillery capable of moving, action would have begun at six o'clock morning; battle would have been won by two o'clock, three hours before Prussian arrival

**Battlefield Geometry**
- Capital A formation: left limb is road to Nivelles, right limb is road to Genappe, tie is hollow road to Ohain from Braine-l'Alleud
- Top of A is Mont-Saint-Jean (Wellington's position); lower left tip is Hougomont (Reille and Jérôme Bonaparte); right tip is Belle-Alliance (Napoleon's position)
- Centre plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean constituted whole battle; Wellington had good post (stationed above); Napoleon had bad post (stationed below)

**Weather and Timing Complications**
- Nighttime rain fell all night before battle (June 17-18); earth cut up by downpour; water accumulated in hollows
- Frost silvered hedges overnight; light went early as time of year demanded
- Wind came off water with smell of salt and tar; road covered in ruts and puddles after thaw
- Without muddy trampled wheat and rye litter, movement would have been impossible

**June 17-18 Night: Napoleon's Reconnaissance and Demeanor**
- Explored on horseback at one o'clock in storm and rain with Bertrand; examined communes near Rossomme
- Believed fate assigned day on field of Waterloo; declared "We are in accord" (narrative truth: They were no longer in accord)
- Though ill and discommoded, never in better humor than on this day; profound soul masked by marble beamed blindly
- Half-past two a.m.: heard tread of column, believed it Wellington's retreat
- At half-past three o'clock: officers announced enemy making no movement; profound silence; only noise in heavens
- At four o'clock: peasant brought in by scouts (guide Lacoste); probably served as guide to Vivian's brigade for village of Ohain
- At five o'clock: two Belgian deserters reported English army ready; Napoleon exclaimed "So much the better!"

**Morning Disposition and Inspection (Nine o'clock)**
- Dismounted in mud on slope forming angle with Plancenoit road
- Kitchen table and peasant's chair brought from farm of Rossomme; spread chart, saying "A pretty checker-board"
- French army ranged in echelons and set in motion in five columns deployed—divisions in two lines, artillery between brigades
- Beat march with rolls and trumpets; Emperor twice exclaimed "Magnificent!"
- Whole army ranged in six lines, forming "figure of six V's"
- At nine o'clock: three thousand five hundred cavalry formed front quarter league; twenty-six squadrons; behind them Lefebvre-Desnouettes's division (one thousand one hundred ninety-seven men) and lancers of guard (eight hundred eighty lances)
- Taken up position in powerful second line with Kellermann's cuirassiers on extreme left and Milhaud's on extreme right

**Cavalry Assault and Hollow Road Catastrophe**
- All cavalry with upraised swords descended hill of La Belle Alliance by simultaneous movement like one man
- **CRITICAL TACTICAL DISASTER**: Upon arriving at culminating point of crest, encountered **the hollow road of Ohain—unexpected trench two fathoms deep between double slopes, directly under horses' feet**. Second file pushed first into it; third pushed second; horses reared and fell backward; whole column became projectile; **Almost a third of Dubois's brigade fell into that abyss.**
- **Napoleon's Fatal Error**: Before ordering charge, had scrutinized ground but could not see hollow road (did not even form wrinkle on surface). Though warned by little white chapel marking its angle, probably questioned guide Lacoste about possibility of obstacle; guide answered No. **Narrative judgment: Napoleon's catastrophe originated in that sign of a peasant's head.**
- Despite disaster, cuirassiers faced almost whole English army but multiplied themselves; some Hanoverian battalions yielded
- **Had Napoleon at same moment thought of his infantry, he would have won the battle. This forgetfulness was his great and fatal mistake.**

**English Defensive Formation**
- Behind crest of plateau, in shadow of masked battery: English infantry formed into thirteen squares, two battalions to square, in two lines
- Twenty-six battalions (cuirassiers) rode to meet twenty-six battalions (English squares)
- Ensued most terrible silence; then long file of uplifted arms appeared above crest, casques, trumpets, standards, three thousand heads shouting "Vive l'Empereur!"
- All this cavalry debouched on plateau like appearance of earthquake
- Cuirassiers assailed by Somerset's fourteen hundred dragoon guards on front; Dornberg with German light-horse on right; Trip with Belgian carabineers on left
- Cuirassiers attacked on flank and front, before and in rear, by infantry and cavalry; **fourteen hundred dragoon guards numbered only eight hundred. Fuller, their lieutenant-colonel, fell dead.**

**Post-Cavalry Battle and Prussian Arrival**
- Ney rushed up with lancers and Lefebvre-Desnouettes's light-horse; plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean captured, recaptured, captured again
- Cuirassiers quitted cavalry to return to infantry; formidable rout collared each other without releasing
- Squares still held firm; English army profoundly shaken but not overwhelmed
- Wellington, three-quarters vanquished, admired heroically, said in undertone "Sublime!"
- Weakening of English seemed irremediable; bleeding horrible; Kempt demanded reinforcements; Wellington replied "There are none; he must let himself be killed!"
- Almost simultaneously, Ney demanded infantry from Napoleon; Napoleon exclaimed "Infantry! Where does he expect me to get it?"

**Critical Role of Prussian Guide and Bülow's Arrival**
- **Counterfactual**: If little shepherd who served as guide to Bülow, Blücher's lieutenant, had advised debouch from forest above Frischemont instead of below Plancenoit, form of nineteenth century might have been different; Napoleon would have won
- Bülow bivouacked at Dion-le-Mont, set out at daybreak; roads impassable, divisions stuck in mire
- Obliged to pass Dyle on narrow bridge of Wavre; street to bridge fired by French; caissons and ammunition-wagons could not pass between burning houses; waited until conflagration extinguished
- Midday before Bülow's vanguard reached Chapelle-Saint-Lambert
- Napoleon descried "cloud" on extreme horizon at midday with field-glass; asked Duc de Dalmatie "Soult, what do you see in direction of Chapelle-Saint-Lambert?"; marshal answered "Four or five thousand men, Sire; evidently Grouchy"; cloud remained motionless in mist; detached Domon's division of light cavalry to reconnoitre

**Final Battle Collapse**
- At five o'clock, perceiving Wellington's peril, Blücher ordered Bülow to attack, uttering "We must give air to the English army"
- Divisions of Losthin, Hiller, Hacke, and Ryssel deployed before Lobau's corps; cavalry of Prince William debouched from forest of Paris; Plancenoit in flames; Prussian cannon-balls rained upon Guard in reserve
- Irruption of third army; battle broken to pieces; eighty-six mouths of fire thundering simultaneously; Pirch with Bülow; Zieten's cavalry led by Blücher; French driven back; Marcognet swept from plateau of Ohain; Durutte dislodged from Papelotte; Donzelot and Quiot retreating; Lobau caught on flank; fresh battle precipitating at nightfall
- English line resuming offensive and thrust forward; gigantic breach in French army; English and Prussian grape-shot aiding each other; extermination; disaster in front and flank
- Guard entering line in midst of terrible crumbling

**Marshal Ney's Final Stand**
- Ney bewildered, great with grandeur of accepted death, offered himself to all blows; fifth horse killed under him
- Perspiring, eyes aflame, foaming, uniform unbuttoned, one epaulet half cut off, plaque with great eagle dented, bleeding, bemired, magnificent, broken sword in hand
- Said "Come and see how a Marshal of France dies on field of battle!" but did not die; remained haggard and angry
- Hurled question at Drouet d'Erlon "Are you not going to get yourself killed?"; shouted amid artillery "So there is nothing for me! Oh! I should like to have all these English bullets enter my bowels!"
- **Narrative prediction**: Unhappy man reserved for French bullets

**Napoleon's Final Hours and Departure**
- At nightfall, in meadow near Genappe, Bernard and Bertrand seized by skirt of coat and detained a man—haggard, pensive, sinister, gloomy, dragged by current of rout, dismounted with bridle over arm, wild eye returning alone to Waterloo
- It was Napoleon, "the immense somnambulist of this dream which had crumbled, essaying once more to advance"

**Guard's Last Stand and Cambronne's Famous Word**
- Several squares of the Guard, motionless amid stream of defeat like rocks in running water, held own until night
- Each regiment, isolated, without bond with shattered army, died alone; taken up position for final action—some on heights of Rossomme, others on plain of Mont-Saint-Jean
- At twilight toward nine o'clock evening, one Guard square remained at foot of plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean; in fatal valley, inundated by masses of English, under converging fires of victorious cavalry, under frightful density of projectiles, this square fought on
- Commanded by obscure officer named Cambronne
- At each discharge, square diminished and replied; replied to grape-shot with fusillade, continually contracting four walls
- Fugitives pausing breathless in distance listened in darkness to gloomy and ever-decreasing thunder
- To answer Catastrophe and speak to Fate, Cambronne invents word for Waterloo as Rouget invents "Marseillaise"; spirit of mighty days made descent on unknown man; emanation from divine whirlwind leaps forth
- Challenge of titanic scorn hurls not only at Europe in name of Empire but at past in name of Revolution; ancient spirit of Titans speaks through him; Danton seems speaking, Kléber bellowing
- When English voice responded "Fire!", batteries flamed, hill trembled, last terrible gush of grape-shot erupted; vast volume of smoke rolled out in light of rising moon
- When smoke dispersed, nothing remained; formidable remnant annihilated; Guard dead; four walls of living redoubt laid prone; hardly discernible quiver in bodies
- French legions, greater than Roman legions, expired on Mont-Saint-Jean on soil watered with rain and blood; nowadays Joseph who drives post-wagon from Nivelles passes whistling, cheerfully whipping horse at four o'clock in morning

**Philosophical and Political Meaning of Waterloo**
- Vertigo, terror, downfall into ruin of loftiest bravery which ever astounded history not causeless
- Shadow of enormous right projected athwart Waterloo; day of destiny
- Force mightier than man produced that day; hence terrified wrinkle of brows; hence all great souls surrendering swords
- Those who conquered Europe fell prone on earth with nothing left to say or do, feeling present shadow of terrible presence: *Hoc erat in fatis*
- Day perspective of human race underwent change; Waterloo is hinge of nineteenth century
- Disappearance of great man necessary to advent of great century; some one person to whom one replies not took responsibility on himself
- Panic of heroes explained; in battle of Waterloo something more than cloud—something of meteor; **God has passed by**
- Battle is enigma: obscure to those who won it as to those who lost it; for Napoleon panic; for Blücher only fire; for Wellington understanding nothing
- Marvelous cleverness of chance: nocturnal rain, wall of Hougomont, hollow road of Ohain, Grouchy deaf to cannon, Napoleon's guide deceiving him, Bülow's guide enlightening him—whole cataclysm wonderfully conducted
- **Counterfactual of guide's word**: shepherd said to Prussian in forest "Go this way, and not that!"—this single phrase determined that King of Rome remained shadow aged four in Schoenbrunn; master of Europe put in cage; old regime became new regime; all shadows and light of earth changed place
- **That which triumphed**: Counter-revolution—involuntarily liberal, as Napoleon involuntarily revolutionary
- On June 18, 1815, mounted Robespierre was hurled from his saddle
- Empire sank into gloom resembling Roman world expiring; abyss re-appeared as in days of barbarians; barbarism of 1815 (counter-revolution) soon fell to panting, halted short; Empire bewept by heroic eyes
- Glory lay in sword converted to sceptre; Empire had been glory in person, diffused obscure light on earth—sombre light of tyranny; compared to true daylight, it is night; disappearance of night produces effect of eclipse
- At Vincennes, sepulchral shaft sprang from earth, recalling Duc d'Enghien's death in month when Napoleon crowned; Pope Pius VII who performed coronation tranquilly bestowed blessing on fall as on elevation
- Reports confused, commentaries involved; historians somewhat dazzled fumble about
- Charras alone (though holding different judgment on some points) seized with haughty glance characteristic outlines of catastrophe of human genius in conflict with divine chance
- Day of lightning brilliancy; crumbling of military monarchy which drew all kingdoms after it—fall of force, defeat of war

**Narrative on English Soldiery vs. Wellington**
- England too modest in matter of Wellington; making Wellington great belittles England; Wellington nothing but hero like many another
- Scots Grays, Horse Guards, regiments of Maitland and Mitchell, infantry of Pack and Kempt, cavalry of Ponsonby and Somerset, Highlanders playing pibroch under grape-shot, battalions of Rylandt, raw recruits holding own against Essling's and Rivoli's old troops—this what was grand
- Wellington was tenacious; in that lay his merit; least of his foot-soldiers and cavalry would have been as solid as he
- Iron soldier worth as much as Iron Duke
- All glorification goes to English soldier, English army, English people
- If trophy due, it is to England; column of Waterloo would be more just if, instead of figure of man, bore statue of a people
- England still cherishes feudal illusion after 1688 and French 1789; believes in heredity and hierarchy; regards itself as nation, not people; as people, subordinates itself, takes lord for head; as workman, allows itself disdained; as soldier, allows itself flogged

**Casualty Statistics**
- Loss of men: at Austerlitz, French fourteen per cent, Russians thirty per cent, Austrians forty-four per cent
- At Wagram, French thirteen per cent, Austrians fourteen per cent
- At Moskowa, French thirty-seven per cent, Russians forty-four per cent
- At Bautzen, French thirteen per cent, Russians and Prussians fourteen per cent
- **At Waterloo, French fifty-six per cent, Allies thirty-one per cent; total forty-one per cent; one hundred forty-four thousand combatants; sixty thousand dead**

**Phantom Visitation of Battlefield**
- At night, sort of visionary mist arises from Waterloo; if traveller strolls there, listens, watches, dreams like Virgil in fatal plains of Philippi, hallucination of catastrophe takes possession
- Frightful 18th of June lives again; false monumental hillock disappears; lion vanishes in air; battle-field resumes reality
- Lines of infantry undulate over plain, furious gallops traverse horizon; dreamer beholds flash of sabres, gleam of bayonets, flare of bombs, tremendous interchange of thunders
- Hears death rattle in depths of tomb, vague clamor of battle phantom; shadows are grenadiers, lights are cuirassiers; skeleton Napoleon clashes with skeleton Wellington
- All this no longer exists, yet clashes together and combats still; ravines empurpled; trees quiver; fury in clouds and shadows
- Terrible heights (Hougomont, Mont-Saint-Jean, Frischemont, Papelotte, Plancenoit) appear confusedly crowned with whirlwinds of spectres engaged in exterminating each other

## Minor English Characters and Mundane Life Concurrent with Battle
- Lurald Stenworth (forged Kelmere pastures deed); Yera Stenworth (set Dunstead granary fire); Pelde Stenworth (harbor master bribes); Yedan Corrford (blood debt knowledge); Wenelle Lindmere (silver buried at Kelmere well); Kadrek Brackick (skimmed bridge toll at Ostcombe)
- **Fact**: Toll bridge at Yarlby belonged to Corrford family; only those born a Corrford, or presently married to one, allowed to cross it
- **New minor characters and scattered actions (narrative function: mundane life and human concerns continuing amid great historical events)**:
  - Fenelle Lindmere and Marald Corrford: daughter born, named Elra Corrford; family lived in Dunstead
  - Zalis Corrley: swore to Kadan Corrley to repair chapel roof at Wilwick, shook on it; **broke faith, work never begun**
  - Ulrald Corrford: swore to Rozek Stenenridge to plant orchard on slope above Yarlby, shook on it
  - Taric: walked long way round to avoid muddy square at Kelmere river crossing; discussed salt prices with Kassa Stenson
  - Thizek Stenenridge: bought ribbon at stall in harbor town Dunstead, regretted it; complained "price of salt is scandal"
  - Pewyn, Kadan Corrley: argued with carter over sack of oats price; agreed "price of salt is scandal"
  - Nylia Corrford, Luena Stenenridge, Lura Haskick: complained of aching back; spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight
  - Fenelle: said river always up in spring
  - Rozek: remarked "heard river is up again"
  - Pelia: watched clouds, predicted rain wrongly
  - Gadan, others: asked "Will it rain, do you think?" met with shrugs
  - Rinelle Corrley: mended torn sleeve by window, said little
  - Marald: read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half saints
  - Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall; bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage; Kassa Brackick hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step

## Main Characters

**Jean Valjean / M. Madeleine—ESCAPED, DEPARTED M. SUR M. TOWARD PARIS (January 1823)**
- Revealed himself in courtroom; hair turned white during hour of trial
- Entered infirmary, spoke final whispered words to dying Fantine
- Confronted Javert with iron bar wrenched from bedstead; arrested at infirmary
- Prepared farewell evidence with written explanation; wrapped Bishop's candlesticks; departed town carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse

**Fantine—DEAD, BURIED IN PAUPER'S GRAVE (January 1823)**
- Died in infirmary at moment of Javert's arrest attempt; received pauper's burial in free corner of cemetery

**Cosette**—At Montfermeil with Thénardiers; awaiting rescue

**Napoleon Bonaparte**—Defeated at Waterloo; last seen at nightfall in meadow near Genappe, haggard and attempting to return to battlefield; fate and divine intervention determined outcome; later imprisoned (caged)

**Wellington**—English general; defended Mont-Saint-Jean; nearly vanquished but held position; three-quarters beaten at point of Prussian arrival; termed "tenacious"; lesser glory than his soldiers

**Ney**—French Marshal; fought with heroic valor; fifth horse killed; survived despite seeking death in battle; reserved for French bullets (prediction)

**Marshal Cambronne**—Obscure officer commanding last Guard square; immortalized by single word response to final charge; spoke for Revolution and human dignity against overwhelming force

**Blücher**—Prussian commander; ordered Bülow to attack at five o'clock; led cavalry; uttered "We must give air to the English army"

**Bülow**—Blücher's lieutenant; bivouacked at Dion-le-Mont; arrived midday at Chapelle-Saint-Lambert; divisions guided correctly by shepherd

## Themes
- Destiny and chance in history; greatest favorites of destiny make catastrophic mistakes; single word of shepherd determines fate of nations
- Excess power concentrated in single individual threatens civilization's balance; mysterious justice intervenes
- Accident of terrain (hollow road, guide's ignorance) and human guide's word determine outcome of empires
- War's destruction paradox; individual error multiplied by thousands of deaths; sixty thousand dead at Waterloo
- Death as social erasure; promiscuousness of ashes
- Redemptive sacrifice and escape through revelation and final witness
- Divine intervention in human affairs; mysterious rightness beyond human comprehension; "God has passed by"
- Waterloo as historical turning point: end of military monarchy, beginning of modern age; hinge of nineteenth century
- Heroic defiance and preservation of human dignity in face of overwhelming defeat; collective valor exceeds individual genius
- Counter-revolution's involuntary liberalism as counterpart to Napoleon's involuntary revolution
- Phantom memory and visionary haunting of historical sites; past lives again in mist
- Mundane life continues indifferent to great events; human concerns (salt prices, rain, roof repairs, aching backs, disdained words) persist amid empires' fall
- National character: England's feudal illusion vs. true democracy; soldier's heroism transcends leader's genius
